title: Continental Chess Presidents Inaugurate World Junior Rapid & Blitz Championships in Al Ain
summary: Al Ain adds a third World Championship milestone to its international chess legacy. The fourth edition of the FIDE World Junior Rapid & Blitz Chess Championships kicked off in Al Ain. Following an intense opening day, five players share the lead in the Open section, and three are tied at the top of the Girls’ standings, all with perfect scores after three rapid rounds.  Held under the patronage of His Highness Sheikh Nahyan bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Sports Council, the championships are organised by the Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club in cooperation with FIDE and the UAE Chess Federation. The event, bringing together 150 players from 40 countries, runs from November 1 to 7 at the Danat Al Ain Resort. The opening ceremony was attended by Sheikh Sultan bin Khalifa bin Sultan bin Shakhbout Al Nahyan, President of the Asian Chess Federation, Chairman of the Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club, and Chairman of the Higher Organising Committee; African Chess Confederation President Bernard Wanjala; and Confederation of Chess for the Americas President José Antonio Carrillo Pujol. Also in attendance were Javier Ochoa de Echagüen, FIDE Honorary Vice-President and President of the Spanish Chess Federation; Hulkar Tohirjonova, President of FIDE’s Central Asian Zone; Özgür Solakoğlu, FIDE Technical Delegate; and representatives of national federations and participating delegations. Following the UAE National Anthem, Sheikh Sultan welcomed the players and delegations, highlighting the championships’ role in bringing young talent together through competition, friendship, and the shared values of concentration, discipline, and sound decision-making. He expressed his gratitude to His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, for his continued support of sport and youth development, and to His Highness Sheikh Hazza bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Ruler’s Representative in the Al Ain Region. He also thanked His Highness Sheikh Nahyan bin Zayed Al Nahyan for his patronage, alongside the Abu Dhabi Sports Council, FIDE, the UAE Chess Federation, and the event’s organising partners. Sheikh Sultan noted that the championships coincide with Al Ain’s designation as the Arab Capital of Tourism for 2026, offering visiting delegations an opportunity to discover the city’s heritage, landmarks, and hospitality. Javier Ochoa delivered the address on behalf of FIDE before Sheikh Sultan officially declared the championships open and joined the distinguished guests in making the ceremonial opening moves on the top Open and Girls’ boards. Perfect starts set the stage for a battle for the lead Five players won all three opening games in the Open section to lead on three points: Artem Uskov (FIDE), India’s Pranav V and Praneeth Vuppala, Kazakhstan’s Satbek Akhmedinov, and Artiom Stribuk. In the Girls’ competition, Kazakhstan’s Zarina Nurgaliyeva, Valeria Kleymenova (FIDE), and Uzbekistan’s Umida Omonova (pictured below) finished the day tied for first place with three points each. Just half a point behind are Eline Roebers of the Netherlands, Aliaksandra Tarasenka of Belarus, and Marina Kuznetsova and Margarita Bendik (both FIDE), setting up closely contested encounters in the coming rounds. Among the UAE players, Hamad Essa Al-Blooshi and Husain Ali Alhammadi each collected two points in the Open section, while Rouda Essa Alserkal scored 1½ points in the Girls’ section. The nine-round rapid competition will conclude on November 4, followed by the blitz events on November 5 and 6.

title: Speed Chess Championship Celebrates 10-Year Anniversary With Live Finals In London
summary:
After 10 years of nail-biting chess, star rivalries, and dramatic matches, we're excited to announce Speed Chess Championship XI (SCC)! The event starts in November and features a $250,000 prize fund, along with up to 150 Champions Chess Tour Leaderboard points.

In 2016, stars such as GMs Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamura, and Fabiano Caruana came together for the first time to play for $40,000 and the title of best online speed chess player. That year, the Speed Chess Championship was born—and the online competitive landscape changed forever.

"Over the past 10 years, the Speed Chess Championship has given fans extraordinary matches, unforgettable comebacks, and the very best players in the world pushing each other to their limits," said Michael Brancato, Chess.com's Events Commissioner. "SCC XI is a celebration of all those moments and the community that gives them meaning."

Fans can join a roaring audience at the live finals in London, England, on February 5 to 7, 2027. The competition will take place at 180 Studios—the same stage where Carlsen defeated GM Alireza Firouzja to claim his fifth title. Get your tickets now and be there for this historic moment for online chess!

Get Your Tickets

Since 2016, the SCC has not only helped professionalize online chess competitions, but it has also become the stage for one of the fiercest rivalries of our time. In all its history, just two players have claimed the title of the world's best online speed chess player. Carlsen won the first two editions, then Nakamura reigned in the speed chess world from 2018 to 2022—his last title coming after a thrilling Final win over the Norwegian. Carlsen then reclaimed the crown in 2023 and won again in 2024 and 2025, matching Nakamura's record.

Nakamura and Carlsen are both returning to play in the SCC this year and, as the world's most prominent speed chess players, are likely to meet again this season. With each player holding five titles, this might be the year one of them finally pulls ahead.

However, the two legends won't be the only players gunning for the title. Speed specialists Firouzja and GM Denis Lazavik, the only two players besides Carlsen to beat Nakamura in an SCC match, are also joining the field. They'll be out for revenge on the world number-one, who beat Lazavik in the 2025 Semifinal and Firouzja in the Final in both 2024 and 2025.

Making his SCC debut is one of the year's most celebrated players, GM Javokhir Sindarov. The Uzbekistani star has had a tremendous year, rising to world number-four. The current World Championship challenger will now look to break Carlsen and Nakamura's grip on the SCC.

Fans can expect to see more of the world's most dangerous speed chess players participating. India's number-one and number-four, GMs Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Nihal Sarin, alongside Turkiye's prodigy GM Yagiz Erdogmus, are joining the action. The United States' number-two and number-three, GMs Caruana and Wesley So; Uzbekistan's number-two GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov; 2024 finalist GM Hans Niemann; blitz specialist GM Dmitry Andreikin; up-and-coming 16-year-old GM Sina Movahed; and former world top-10 GM Vladislav Artemiev round out the field.

The event will follow the traditional format that has captivated players and fans alike. Sixteen of the world's best players will compete in a knockout, with every match featuring two blitz and one bullet section.

Since its debut, the SCC has grown into Chess.com's most prestigious event. From an experimental online showdown between elite grandmasters, the event has evolved into an esports spectacle, complete with a live audience cheering for their heroes. Now, it is a critical stepping stone to the world's largest esports competition, the Esports World Cup (EWC)—winning the SCC nets 150 CCT Leaderboard points, a considerable advantage for players seeking one of 12 EWC spots coming from the CCT.

Who do you think will win the Speed Chess Championship XI? Let us know in the comments below!

title: KazChess Masters: Lazavik takes title, Smirnov earns GM norm
summary:
Denis Lazavik won the KazChess Masters in Almaty with 6½/9 points, finishing unbeaten after drawing his final-round game against Aram Hakobyan. The 19-year-old Belarusian overtook Daniil Dubov in the penultimate round and eventually finished half a point ahead of the Russian. Another notable result came from 14-year-old Kazakh IM Mark Smirnov, who scored 5½/9, shared third place with Shamsiddin Vokhidov and earned his first GM norm. | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE (World Rapid and Blitz Team Championships 2026)

Lazavik overtakes Dubov in final stretch

Denis Lazavik won the KazChess Masters in Almaty, finishing the nine-round tournament with 6½ points and an unbeaten record of four wins and five draws. The 19-year-old Belarusian GM secured outright first place by drawing his final game against Aram Hakobyan.

Daniil Dubov finished second on 6/9, while Shamsiddin Vokhidov and 14-year-old Kazakh IM Mark Smirnov shared third place with 5½ points. Smirnov was another of the tournament's notable performers, earning his first GM norm.

Dubov entered the final three rounds as the sole leader , half a point ahead of Lazavik and Vokhidov. However, the 30-year-old from Moscow failed to make the most of a clearly advantageous endgame and was held to a draw by Sauat Nurgaliyev in round seven, while Lazavik defeated Alua Nurman with the black pieces to catch him on 5/7.

The following day, Lazavik took the lead by defeating Nurgaliyev with white. Dubov, meanwhile, drew with Hakobyan, leaving him half a point behind the Belarusian going into the final round. Vokhidov also won his eighth-round game, against Nurman, to join Dubov on 5½/8 and remain in the battle for overall victory.

All three frontrunners had the black pieces in Tuesday's final round. Dubov was the first to finish, drawing against top seed Mahammad Muradli after 31 moves. Vokhidov, meanwhile, suffered a surprise defeat against Nurgaliyev, the 16-year-old Kazakh IM who had entered the round without a victory.

Lazavik consequently needed only a draw to secure the title. Hakobyan pressed for some time in a minor-piece endgame, trying to exploit Black's isolated pawn, but the Belarusian held the position without major difficulties. The players agreed to a draw after 58 moves, confirming Lazavik as the tournament winner.

The result adds another classical tournament victory to Lazavik's record, following his triumph at the Abu Dhabi Masters in 2025. The youngster, who is a formidable online blitz and bullet player, reached the final of this year's Esports World Cup, where he lost to Magnus Carlsen .

Denis Lazavik holding the winner's trophy after emerging victorious at the strong 2025 Abu Dhabi Masters | Photo: Aditya Sur Roy / ChessBase India

Another notable result came from Smirnov, the youngest and lowest-rated participant in the ten-player field. After losing his opening game against Dubov, the Kazakh youngster recovered to score four wins and three draws from his remaining eight encounters, with his only other defeat coming against Vokhidov.

Smirnov finished with victories over compatriots Edgar Mamedov and Denis Makhnev in rounds seven and nine, both with the black pieces. His final score of 5½/9 corresponded to a tournament performance rating of 2666 and secured his first GM norm. The 2024 under-12 world champion thus added another achievement to his growing list of successful results.

A first GM norm for Mark Smirnov! | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

title: FIDE President Timur Turlov meets Akaki Iashvili to discuss future events and chess development
summary: FIDE President Timur Turlov held a meeting with Akaki Iashvili, President of the Georgian Chess Federation and Representative of the FIDE President for Special Projects, to discuss a wide range of strategic matters related to the development of international chess, the organisation of major competitions, and new initiatives for the coming years. The meeting covered the recent FIDE elections in Uzbekistan and the World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, with particular attention given to sporting results, organisational matters and the overall execution of the event. A significant part of the discussion focused on the international chess calendar for 2027–2028, including World Championships and other events falling within the scope of the FIDE Events Commission. The two officials exchanged views on possible improvements to competition formats, organisational standards and the overall experience for players, organisers, spectators and media. A number of new ideas and initiatives are currently being considered with the aim of further raising the quality and appeal of major FIDE events. Chess development in Georgia The meeting also addressed the current projects and strategic plans of the Georgian Chess Federation. One of the key topics was the major reconstruction of the Tbilisi Chess Palace, a landmark chess venue located in the center of the Georgian capital. The renovation and restoration works are expected to be completed by the end of 2027. Another area of discussion was the development of chess in preschool education. A project introducing chess to young children is already being implemented in 15 kindergartens in the Georgian city of Poti. The initiative was highlighted as a model with potential for further development and possible adaptation in other countries. New social initiative: chess for miners The meeting also touched upon a new social initiative aimed at bringing chess to workers in the coal-mining industry. Among the ideas discussed was the possibility of organising the first World Chess Championship for Miners. Given the active coal mines in the city of Tkibuli, Georgia could play a pivotal role in the development of such a project. The initiative reflects the broader objective of expanding the social reach of chess and creating new opportunities for people from different professional and social backgrounds to engage with the game. Expanding chess globally A substantial part of the discussion was dedicated to the continued development of chess across all continents. Timur Turlov and Akaki Iashvili discussed ways to broaden the geographic reach of international competitions, strengthen support for national federations, develop new chess projects, and deepen international cooperation. Particular attention was given to countries and regions where chess already has a strong foundation but retains considerable potential for further growth. The meeting concluded with an agreement to continue working closely on these areas and to develop practical proposals for new projects and improvements to FIDE competitions in the coming years.
